intro: A quiet Romanza contains a recognisable quotation from Mendelssohn’s Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage. Its three asterisks leave the dedicatee less certain than the other portraits.
question: What can a quotation suggest without settling a person’s identity?

sections.mNote: a gently moving phrase introduces the portrait

sections.label: The quieter seascape
sections.mNote: Mendelssohn is quoted within a much softer texture

cues.title: Motion under a quiet melody
cues.text: The clarinet begins above moving second violins and cellos. Listen for the difference between the melody’s relatively long notes and the little waves of accompaniment underneath.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 87, rehearsal 55: clarinet melody, moving second violins and cellos, with other instruments joining later in the phrase.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A portrait with asterisks
cues.text: The Elgar Society identifies Lady Mary Lygon as the probable subject, but the three asterisks do not establish her name beyond doubt. The alternative suggestion of Helen Weaver remains a hypothesis, not a second documented dedicatee.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society explicitly qualifies Mary Lygon as probable and discusses the competing Weaver theory. No claim of certain identity or a literal voyage by the dedicatee is made. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: Mendelssohn at sea
cues.text: The Romanza quotes Mendelssohn’s overture Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage. The borrowed phrase supplies a musical association with the sea; it is not proof of who the unnamed person is or where she is travelling.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies the quotation. Novello p. 88 places quotation marks around the clarinet phrase over soft timpani; the timestamp is contextual, not the quotation’s onset. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: The quiet is sustained
cues.text: The final part gradually retreats into a very soft recorded span. Listen for how much motion can continue inside a quiet texture instead of waiting only for another large orchestral attack.
cues.evidence: The report falls through 1:40–2:00 and remains low towards the ending, after the much stronger 1:05–1:15 span.

transitions.title: The texture makes space for a quotation
transitions.how: A poco rallentando leads to tranquillo. The texture becomes very soft: violas move quietly while timpani sustain a roll, and the solo clarinet introduces the quoted Mendelssohn phrase. The quotation enters inside a thinning texture rather than as a grand announcement.
transitions.evidence: Novello p. 88, rehearsal 56. The strongest report boundary is 0:18; the ensuing 0:25–0:50 span is markedly quiet. This anchors the whole transition, not the clarinet’s first quoted note.

transitions.title: The Romanza gathers weight again
transitions.how: The subdued quotation passage gives way to a more expansive Romanza phrase. Moving string accompaniment and fuller wind support restore forward motion, and the dynamic grows before the music returns to its quiet ending.
transitions.evidence: Novello pp. 89–92 develop the Romanza material. The report changes at 1:02 and rises towards a 1:10 crest; no exact bar is assigned.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 87–92, rehearsal figures 55–60. Whole-variation passage map: the 0:18 and 1:02 changes, the strong 1:05–1:15 span, and the quiet final minute distinguish the Romanza, quotations and expansion. No precise quotation onset is asserted.

timeline.note: Clarinet begins over gently moving second violins and cellos (p. 87).
The first Romanza phrase spreads through the wind and string parts with restrained horn support (p. 87).
Solo clarinet introduces the quiet quotation above timpani and subdued strings; other desks gradually withdraw (p. 88).
The very soft quotation passage leaves the clarinet exposed above moving viola and sustained cello support (p. 89).
The central expansion gains brass and timpani weight as the recorded level rises (p. 90).
The Romanza resumes its more lightly scored wind-and-string motion after the larger swell (pp. 90–91).
The final quotation is prepared by another thinning of the texture and a quiet timpani roll (p. 92).
Clarinet and the soft lower-string texture remain after upper strings, horns and basses release (p. 92).

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
